system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2175-09-17 02:01:00 to 2175-09-20 11:15:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: James, a man with a history of COPD, alcohol dependence, and chronic pain from prior trauma, was admitted after returning to the emergency department with severe shortness of breath and alcohol intoxication. He had left AMA the prior day but returned due to worsening respiratory symptoms. Imaging showed recurrent right middle lobe collapse and findings consistent with acute on chronic aspiration, but no malignancy. He was treated for a COPD exacerbation with oral steroids and antibiotics, and for alcohol withdrawal with diazepam and supportive vitamins. His sodium normalized with oral hydration, and he was weaned off oxygen. Despite clinical improvement, he elected to leave against medical advice on hospital day two, declining discharge medications and follow-up instructions due to dissatisfaction with pain management. He was warned of the risks of untreated withdrawal and respiratory decline.
problems: Acute alcoholic intoxication in alcoholism, unspecified

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. James, I’m Dr. Reyes. You’re in the hospital because you came in with trouble breathing and were found to be intoxicated. Can I ask what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You’re wasting my time. Read the chart. I’ve been here 12 times in six months. I don’t need this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand you’re frustrated. But I need to make sure you’re safe. You were coughing up green mucus and short of breath. Is that still bothering you?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I can’t catch my breath. But I don’t want you poking around. Just give me oxygen and let me go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you oxygen and treatments for your lungs. But you also had a high alcohol level. That can cause serious problems if it drops too fast. We need to monitor you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know my body. I don’t need babysitting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. But last time you left early, your breathing got worse. We’re here to help you avoid that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows some scarring and collapsed areas in your lungs. It’s likely from not using your inhalers and from drinking. We’re treating it with steroids and antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I forgot the inhalers. I’ve been drinking a pint a day. So what?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s part of why you’re sick. Alcohol weakens your lungs and immune system. It also increases your risk of aspiration—breathing stomach contents into your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been doing it for years. I’m not stopping now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m not judging. But right now, your body is struggling. We’re giving you medications to calm your airways and fight infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood work came back. White count is normal, no sign of severe infection. But you have high lymphocytes—your body’s reacting to something, maybe the alcohol or lung irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m fine. Can I leave?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. Your alcohol level was very high. Now that it’s dropping, you could have withdrawal—seizures, confusion, even delirium tremens. We’re giving you medication to prevent that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been through it before. I can handle it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I believe you. But it’s dangerous. We’re also giving you thiamine and folic acid—alcohol depletes these, and low levels can cause brain damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on a nicotine patch and gum. You’ve smoked a pack a day for years. Quitting will help your lungs heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve tried. Nothing works.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s hard. But every day without smoking helps. We’ll keep supporting you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing is a little better. Oxygen level is 96% on two liters. Still some crackles in your lungs, but less coughing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I want to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re improving, but you’re still at risk. Your blood pressure is high—155 over 93. That’s from withdrawal and your usual hypertension. We’re continuing your blood pressure meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My BP’s always high. I don’t care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It matters because it strains your heart. We’ll check it again when you’re stable to see if your usual meds are enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CIWA score is up—22. That means withdrawal symptoms are worse: tremors, anxiety. We’re adjusting your diazepam dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel shaky. My skin’s crawling. But I don’t want more meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This dose will help. Skipping it could lead to seizures. We’ve seen it before. I don’t want that for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fine. But I’m leaving soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine test showed no infection. Dark urine is likely from dehydration and alcohol. We’re encouraging fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t like the hospital water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can get you something else. Staying hydrated helps your liver and kidneys process the alcohol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing’s better. You’re on less oxygen—just two liters. Still some ronchi, but your cough is looser.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I told you I’d get better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You are, but it’s the treatment helping. If you stop now, you could crash again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’d like you to go to extended care after this—some rehab support for alcohol and lungs. What do you think?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No way. I’m not going to rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not mandatory. But it could help you stay out of the hospital. You’ve been here a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know my pattern. I’ll go home, drink, get sick, come back. That’s how it is.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear that. But each time, it gets riskier. Your lungs are weaker. One bad episode could be fatal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last night, your oxygen was 99% on two liters. Still some wet breath sounds, but you’re moving air better. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Still tired. But I’m ready to leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But you’re still in withdrawal. Leaving now puts you at risk for seizures or delirium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve done it before. I’ll take my chances.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But I need you to know: if you leave, we can’t give you the full course of antibiotics or steroids. Your lungs may flare again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Give me the pills. I’ll take them at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can give you some, but you’ll need a follow-up. And please, no more alcohol until you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do what I want.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve signed out against medical advice. Your condition is stable—alert, breathing well, blood pressure controlled. But you’re still at risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know the risks. I’m leaving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Take these meds: prednisone for five days, azithromycin for five days, and keep using your inhalers. The nicotine patch is now 14 mg—step down as you can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you have shaking, confusion, or trouble breathing, come back immediately. Please consider calling the rehab center. They can help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll think about it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself, Mr. James. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah. Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse says you’re getting dressed. Just a final check—your vitals are stable: 98.9°F, BP 159/91, pulse 60, oxygen 99% on two liters.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel okay. Just want out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re alert and walking fine. But please, if you feel worse, don’t wait. Come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will if I have to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And use the albuterol inhaler every four hours as needed. Don’t skip it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take the discharge papers. They explain everything. Please read them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll look at them later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright. Be safe, Mr. James.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: He’s leaving against medical advice. Vitals stable, alert, ambulatory. Discharge instructions given.

summary.summary_paragraph: James, a man with a history of COPD, alcohol dependence, and tobacco use, was admitted for shortness of breath and alcohol intoxication. He was initially agitated and uncooperative but gradually stabilized with treatment for a COPD exacerbation, including steroids, bronchodilators, and antibiotics. He showed signs of alcohol withdrawal, requiring diazepam and supportive vitamins. His breathing improved, and oxygen needs decreased, but he continued to experience withdrawal symptoms. Despite medical advice, he chose to leave against medical advice on the fourth day, declining further monitoring or rehab referral. He was discharged on oral medications with instructions to continue treatment at home.
problems: Acute alcoholic intoxication in alcoholism, continuous
